en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Jewel Chapter 83.
The Training Rule on the Inner Apartment.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala commanded his park-keeper: "Go, my good man, and clear the park; we shall go to the park.
"Yes, Your Majesty," the park-keeper replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala, and while clearing the park, he saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a certain tree.
Having seen him, he approached King Pasenadi of Kosala and, having approached, said to King Pasenadi of Kosala: "The park is empty, Your Majesty, but the Blessed One is sitting there.
"Very well, my good man; we shall wait upon the Blessed One ourselves.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went to the park and approached the Blessed One. Now at that time, a certain lay follower was sitting waiting upon the Blessed One.
King Pasenadi of Kosala saw that lay follower sitting there attending upon the Blessed One. Upon seeing him, he stood there terrified.
Then it occurred to King Pasenadi of Kosala: “This man cannot be an evil person, since he attends upon the Blessed One.
He approached the Blessed One; having approached, [he addressed] the Blessed One...
Having paid homage, he sat down to one side.
Then that lay follower, out of respect for the Blessed One, neither paid homage to King Pasenadi of Kosala nor rose up for him.
Thereupon, King Pasenadi of Kosala was displeased, thinking: “How can this man...”
“When I have arrived, this man will neither bow down to me nor rise up for me.

Then the Blessed One, perceiving that King Pasenadi of Kosala was displeased, said to King Pasenadi of Kosala: “Great king, this lay follower is learned, one who has mastered the traditional teachings, and is free from passion for sensual pleasures.
Then it occurred to King Pasenadi of Kosala: “This lay follower does not deserve to be treated as insignificant, since even the Blessed One speaks in praise of him.”
He said this to that lay follower: “Lay follower, you may say whatever you need.
“Very well, Your Majesty,” he replied.
Then the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, and inspired King Pasenadi of Kosala with a discourse on the Dhamma.
He inspired and gladdened him. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having been instructed, urged, inspired,
and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One,
and keeping him to his right, departed.
Now at that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala had gone up to the top of his excellent palace. King Pasenadi of Kosala saw that lay follower walking along the carriage road with a parasol in his hand.
Having seen him, he had him summoned and said this: “It is said, lay follower, that you are learned and a master of the traditional texts.
It would be well, lay follower, if you were to teach the Dhamma to our women’s quarters.”
“Your Majesty, I know by the word of the noble ladies that they themselves will teach the Dhamma to the king’s harem.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, thinking, “The lay follower has spoken the truth,” approached the Blessed One;
having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the king...
Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One:
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would command a single bhikkhu who might teach the Dhamma to our women’s quarters.
Then the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Pasenadi of Kosala with a discourse on the Dhamma... [as before] ...and having circumambulated him to the right, he departed.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “In that case, Ānanda, teach the Dhamma to the king’s harem.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. From time to time he entered and taught the Dhamma to the king’s harem.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of King Pasenadi of Kosala.
Now at that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala was lying on his bed with Queen Mallikā.
Queen Mallikā saw the Venerable Ānanda approaching from afar. Upon seeing him, she rose up suddenly, and her yellow, polished garment slipped off.
Then the Venerable Ānanda turned back right there, went to the monastery, and reported this matter to the monks.
Those monks who were of few desires... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the Venerable Ānanda enter the king’s inner palace without having been informed in advance? ...
[and so on] ... "Is it true, Ānanda, that you enter the king’s inner palace without having been informed in advance?"
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, Ānanda, enter the royal palace without first having been announced?”
"This, Ānanda, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him...
and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:"
“Monks, there are these ten dangers in entering a royal palace.
What are the ten?
Here, monks, a king is seated together with his chief queen, and a monk enters there.”
Either the queen, seeing the bhikkhu, displays a smile;
or the bhikkhu, seeing the queen, displays a smile.
Thereupon, it occurs to the king:
‘Surely they have done something for these people, or they will do so.
This, monks, is the first danger in entering a king’s inner palace.
Furthermore, monks, a king has many duties and much to be done.
Having gone to a certain woman, he does not remember it.
She becomes pregnant by him.
Then this thought occurs to the king:
‘No one else enters here except for one who has gone forth.
Could this be an offense for one who has gone forth?
This, monks, is the second danger in entering a royal palace.
Furthermore, monks, suppose some treasure is lost in the king’s inner palace.
Then it occurs to the king:
“No one else enters here except for a renunciant.”
"Could there not be work for one who has gone forth?
This, monks, is the third danger in entering a king’s inner palace.
Furthermore, monks, secret counsels within the king’s inner palace leak out to the outside.
Then it occurs to the king:
"No one else enters here except for one who has gone forth.
Could this be the work of one who has gone forth?"
This, monks, is the fourth danger in entering a king’s inner palace.
Furthermore, monks, in a king’s inner palace, either the son longs for the father or the father longs for the son;
it occurs to them thus: [“I will kill him”].
‘Indeed, no one else enters here except for one who has gone forth.
Could it be that there might be some offense for one who has gone forth?
This, monks, is the fifth danger in entering a royal palace.
Furthermore, monks, a king appoints one of low station to a high position.
Those who find this disagreeable think:
“The king is indeed associating with a renunciant.”
"Could there not be work for one who has gone forth?
This, monks, is the sixth danger in entering a king's inner palace.
Furthermore, monks, a king may appoint someone of high station to a low position.
Those for whom this was unpleasant thought:
“The king is indeed associating with one who has gone forth. Could this be the doing of the renunciant?”
This, monks, is the seventh danger in entering a royal palace.
Furthermore, monks, a king may dispatch his army at an improper time.
Those for whom this is unpleasant think thus:
“The king is indeed intimately associated with one who has gone forth.
Could this not lead to trouble for the one who has gone forth?
This, monks, is the eighth disadvantage in entering a royal palace.
Furthermore, monks, when a king has dispatched his army at the proper time and then turns it back from midway on the road,
those for whom this is unpleasant think:
"The king is indeed associating with one who has gone forth."
"Could there not be work for one who has gone forth?
This, monks, is the ninth danger in entering a king’s inner palace.

Furthermore, monks, in a king’s inner palace there is the crushing of elephants, the crushing of horses, and the crushing of chariots, as well as forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects that are alluring, which are not suitable for one who has gone forth.
“Monks, this is the tenth disadvantage in entering a royal palace.
These, monks, are the ten disadvantages in entering a royal palace.
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked the Venerable Ānanda in many ways for being difficult to support... [and so forth].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:

“Whosoever monk, without prior announcement, should pass beyond the threshold pillar of a consecrated Khattiya king while the king has not yet departed and the regalia have not yet been removed, it is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
Whosoever, moreover:
Whoever is such a person … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”

A khattiya is one who is well-born on both sides, from the mother’s side and the father’s side, of pure descent, unblemished and irreproachable by birth as far back as the seventh generation of ancestors.
He is one who has been consecrated by coronation.
He has been consecrated with the kṣatriya consecration.
"While the king has not departed" means that the king has not yet left his bedchamber.
"Aniggataratanakā" means that the chief queen has not emerged from her bedchamber, or both have not emerged.
"Previously unannounced" means...
Without having first taken leave.
What is called an "indakhīla" is the threshold of a bedchamber.
A "bedchamber" (sayanighara) is any place where a bed has been prepared for a king, even if it is merely enclosed by a screen-wall.
"Should he cross the threshold" (indakhīlaṃ atikkāmeyya): [this refers to the boundary of the royal precinct].
If he steps over the threshold with the first foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he steps over the second foot, there is an offense entailing expiation.
If he has not informed [the owner] and perceives that he has not informed, and he steps over the doorpost, there is an offense entailing expiation.
If he passes beyond the threshold pillar when it has not been announced, and he is in doubt, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If he passes beyond the threshold pillar when it has not been announced, but he perceives that it has been announced, there is an offense of expiation.
If it has been announced, but he perceives that it has not been announced, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it has been informed and he is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it has been informed and he perceives that it has been informed, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
If he has not been acknowledged [as such],
he is not a kshatriya,
nor is he one consecrated by the kshatriya consecration.
The king has emerged from his bedchamber,
the chief queen has emerged from her bedchamber,
or both have emerged.
Not in a sleeping-quarters building;
except for one who is insane,
or for one who is the first offender.
The training rule on the inner apartments is finished; this is the first.
